title: How much is left when one part goes from ten of twenty seven?
description: A strip is cut into twenty seven equal parts and ten of them are shaded. One shaded part is taken away, and the answer is written in lowest terms using the biggest common factor.
teaching_notes: One idea: when two fractions count the same size of part, take away the top numbers, keep the bottom number, then divide the top and the bottom by their biggest common factor. Watch for students who stop at the first fraction without making it smaller.

video_script.why: The child takes away fractions that count the same fractional unit by taking away parts of one strip, then writes the answer in lowest terms with the biggest common factor.
video_script.substitution: The same rectangular strip as the book's solved question about sevenths, now cut into twenty seven equal parts.
video_script.anchor: a rectangular strip cut into twenty seven equal parts with ten parts shaded, as in the book
video_script.payoff_line: Ten twenty sevenths take away one twenty seventh is nine twenty sevenths, which is one third

final_answer.spoken: nine twenty sevenths, which is one third

video_script.fraction_reading: ten twenty sevenths, one twenty seventh, nine twenty sevenths, one third, five sixths, one sixth
never_show: the remaining fraction before the answer beat
maths_rules: the strip is cut into 27 equal parts, so each part is 1/27; 10/27 is 10 shaded parts
10/27 and 1/27 count the same fractional unit 1/27, so the numerators are taken away: 10 − 1 = 9
9 and 27 have the biggest common factor 9: 9/27 = (9 ÷ 9)/(27 ÷ 9) = 1/3
check: 9 parts left + 1 part taken away = 10 parts, which is 10/27
ground demo: 5/6 − 4/6 = 1/6 on a strip of 6 equal parts
video_script.design: One idea: same size of part, take away the tops, keep the bottom, then divide by the biggest common factor. The strip stays on the board from start to end.
